TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
FRIDAY, 03 JULY 2026
AT 10:00AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 3, DAY 5
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC, COMMISSIONER
RICHARD LANCASTER SC WITH MATT SHERMAN AND
CHRISTOPHER BESHARA, COUNSEL ASSISTING

<THE HEARING COMMENCED AT 10.00 AM
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Commissioner, I call Sarah Vandenbroek.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Will I take an oath or make an affirmation?
MS VANDENBROEK: Make an affirmation.
<SARAH VANDENBROEK, AFFIRMED
MR LANCASTER SC: Ms Vandenbroek, what's your full name, please?
MS VANDENBROEK: Sarah Vandenbroek.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have prepared two statements and provided them to
the Commission. The first is dated 9 June 2026. Are the contents of that statement
true and correct?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, they do.
MR LANCASTER SC: Commissioner, that bears the ID STA.0326.0001.0001 and
I tender that statement.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, that statement will be marked as an exhibit.
MR LANCASTER SC: Ms Vandenbroek, you have also prepared a more recent
statement dated 26 June 2026 which has been prepared in a redacted form. Are the
contents of that statement true and correct?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Commissioner, I tender the redacted version of the
statement for present purposes, DTR.8999.0002.0001.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, the redacted second statement will also be received as an
exhibit.
MR LANCASTER SC: Ms Vandenbroek, you are a First Assistant Secretary in the
Department of Infrastructure, Transport Regional Development, Communications,
Sport and the Arts?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: That's a division - within the Department, you are
responsible for an Online Safety and Classification division; is that right?

MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that's the division of the Department responsible for
the regulation of digital platforms and for online safety?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: You commenced work in that division September 2024.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, I did.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, as First Assistant Secretary with responsibility for
digital platforms, do you have a general understanding of the business model of
social media platforms that operate in Australia?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, I do.
MR LANCASTER SC: How do social media companies generate revenue from
providing content and services to Australian users?
MS VANDENBROEK: I understand the majority of revenue is generated through
advertising. Some have subscriptions and other arrangements in place depending on
the nature of the service. Some of the platforms have - particularly the gaming
platforms have in-game purchases, but for the main social media platforms, it is
largely advertising revenue.
MR LANCASTER SC: Attracting new users and increasing the use of the platforms
by existing users is central to the model of those main social media platforms; is that
your understanding?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes. It is attracting and retaining users and maximising the
time that users engage with the platform.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes, the display of advertisements to individuals in
Australia engaging with or interacting with the social media platform generates
revenue. So those interactions might include viewing or sharing or commenting on
content; is that right?
MS VANDENBROEK: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is it your understanding that, as a general proposition, the
more eyes a social media has on the service that it provides, the more revenue it can
stand to make from advertisers who wish to advertise to Australian users?
MS VANDENBROEK: That's my understanding.

MR LANCASTER SC: Do you understand that to create a financial incentive to
have content on the service that is either interesting or controversial because, in
either case, interactions with that content will increase?
MS VANDENBROEK: That is my understanding, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And do you understand that to include a financial incentive
for social media platforms to promote or acquiesce in the spread of harmful content
online because it is likely to be, or more likely to be controversial or shared or
commented on?
MS VANDENBROEK: That's my understanding.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is that a key challenge that must be managed by the
government in designing effective laws to regulate social media platforms?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, it is certainly something the government is interested
in looking at.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have given evidence in your first statement about the
Rickard Review?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And the Online Safety Act complaint provision that
required an independent review to be undertaken of the operation of the statute
within three years of its commencement?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Ms Rickard was appointed to undertake the independent
review?
MS VANDENBROEK: She was.
MR LANCASTER SC: And Ms Rickard is herself a very experienced regulator?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: She was the deputy - a deputy chair of the ACCC?
MS VANDENBROEK: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Prior to that, she held senior roles within ASIC.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.

MR LANCASTER SC: And she was awarded the Public Service Medal herself in
2011.
MS VANDENBROEK: She was.
MR LANCASTER SC: The Rickard Review was announced by the government on
22 November 2023.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And the review ran for nearly a year.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And she was supported by a secretariat within your
Department?
MS VANDENBROEK: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And an issues paper was published in April 2024.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Stakeholders were given an opportunity to make
submissions about that issues paper?
MS VANDENBROEK: They were.
MR LANCASTER SC: There was extensive stakeholder engagement during the
review process?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that involved engagement from social media
platforms?
MS VANDENBROEK: It did, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I bring up Ms Rickard's final report. It's
EWR.5999.0001.0039. And if we could go to PDF page 27, please. In the bottom
half of the page, there's an overview of the review process set out and you see
Ms Rickard received 2200 responses at the top of the right-hand column.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.

MR LANCASTER SC: There was an extensive process of consultation that set out
in the bullet points in the right-hand column, including 72 meetings that she held
with stakeholders.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And she held seven round tables?
MS VANDENBROEK: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, if we go to PDF page 198, please, Appendix C of the
document. This is an appendix that sets out a list of the individuals and organisations
who were consulted and they include all of the major platforms.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And then if we go to the next page, page 199, there are
a series of round tables were held.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And a roundtable was - that included roundtables with
community groups that were regarded as disproportionately impacted by online
harms.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: The Executive Council of Australian Jewry, among others,
was consulted.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, Ms Rickard was required to report by 31 October
2024, with which she complied.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: We got almost to page 200 in the document on the screen;
it was a long and detailed discussion of the issues.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, it was.
MR LANCASTER SC: And it provided a series of recommendations to the
government for review or amendment of the Online Safety Act.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.

MR LANCASTER SC: And they included recommendations in three particular
areas: a digital duty of care, introduction of a definition of online hate, and changes
to the Adult Cyber Abuse Scheme.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now - just pardon me for a moment. The Government
has - the Commonwealth Government has published a response to the Rickard
Review.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that response was published on 14 April this year,
2026.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, that's right.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can you explain, please, to the Commissioner the
circumstances that led to it being 18 months between the provision of the report to
the government and the delivery of the government response?
MS VANDENBROEK: Certainly. There was a lot of detail to work through. As you
would know, there were 67 recommendations in the report. They are very detailed,
very wide-ranging. We had to work through them in tranches to understand what the
practical implications would be of implementing them, and, indeed, whether it made
sense to implement all of them where some may overlap. We worked with other
government agencies and with the eSafety Commissioner's team and with our
Minister's office to form positions on those recommendations. We also had to take
into account other work that was underway, including a reform of the classification
scheme that was in progress at the time.
And we had to look at how we could sensibly sequence the work. It wouldn't have
been feasible to try to implement all 67 recommendations at once. The government
had already announced an intention to focus on the digital duty of care, so we were
progressing that work as well. We were also very much focused on the social media
minimum age work. So it did take time to work through the plan with regard to all of
the recommendations.
MR LANCASTER SC: Ms Vandenbroek, can I just ask you to speak up a little.
MS VANDENBROEK: Sorry.
MR LANCASTER SC: The transcriber is having a little difficulty with your soft
voice.
MS VANDENBROEK: Sorry, I will try to speak louder.

MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. You referred to the work the Department was
doing at the same time on the social media minimum age -
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: - reforms. Those changes came into effect on 10 December
2025, as I understand it?
MS VANDENBROEK: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: But the legislation for that purpose was passed on 27
November 2024.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, that's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: So there was - the work required to be done by
departmental officers was in the context of - not of developing the legislation for
social media minimum age, because that had already been put in place in November
2024.
MS VANDENBROEK: That is correct. We were focused on the media campaign
and the awareness raising, working with the eSafety Commissioner on the regulatory
guidance and just generally raising awareness.
MR LANCASTER SC: How many officers within your branch were involved in the
task of considering and preparing the response to the Rickard Review?
MS VANDENBROEK: There is a core team of eight or nine staff. It has changed
over time, depending on whether we have a graduate in the team or not. They were
the same team that were responsible for the early work on the digital duty of care.
MR LANCASTER SC: And they were the same team that - as you have explained
it, at the same time was considering the response to the Rickard Review, they were
otherwise progressing consideration of the digital duty of care; is that what
happened?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes. Yes, the same team worked on the Rickard Review
and the duty of care.
MR LANCASTER SC: You accept that it's the eSafety who is responsible for
administering the legislation as it applies to the social media minimum age?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, that's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: So departmental officers weren't engaged in that aspect of
those provisions?

MS VANDENBROEK: No. No, we weren't.
MR LANCASTER SC: Do you consider that the branch that you lead was not
adequately resourced to manage platform policy in a timely way because it took that
18-month period to develop a governmental response to the Rickard Review?
MS VANDENBROEK: No, I think it was more the complexity, and there was also
an election during that period, which meant a change of Minister for our portfolio. So
we had a caretaker period where we couldn't work with the Minister's office and then
we had a new Minister. There was a process of briefing the new Minister and the
new office on the review, so a lot of the work that was done when the report was first
handed over was then redone with the new office to make them familiar with the
recommendations and the content, which is quite extensive.
So that contributed to the delay, and then it was the availability of various
stakeholders and legal advice. We have a fabulous legal team in the Department but
we put a lot of pressure on them from a lot of angles so we couldn't ask for everyone
to be done all at once.
MR LANCASTER SC: Could I bring up the text of the response, please, which has
the ID RCD.0001.0001.0193. This is the government response which, I think, ran to
some 16 pages.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, that's right.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes, if we go to PDF page 3, in this context, there's an
indication of the government's short form response to each of the recommendations,
which support, support in principle, note, or not support.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, the support in principle category says is used where:
"...the government supports the intent or merit of the recommendation but considers
that there are other more effective ways to deliver on this intent, or where further
consideration is required to consider implementation, resourcing and prioritisation
options."
So support in principle might include circumstances in which the recommendation
gets taken no further?
MS VANDENBROEK: It does. The support in principle indicates that we may or
may not. It's not closing the door on any of the recommendations; it means we need
to do further work to determine whether it will be taken forward or not.

MR LANCASTER SC: Or if there are other options for implementation, resourcing
or prioritisation, perhaps doing nothing is incorporated within the support in
principle category?
MS VANDENBROEK: It can be, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: The note category refers to further analysis being required?
MS VANDENBROEK: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And not supported is clear. In respect of the note category
which suggests further analysis is required, or support in principle, which refers to
further consideration, has any further consideration or analysis occurred?
MS VANDENBROEK: For some of the recommendations, yes. For others, we
haven't got to them yet.
MR LANCASTER SC: In respect of those that have been further considered, is
there any development or update on the government response to the
recommendations -
MS VANDENBROEK: We haven't -
MR LANCASTER SC: - that you can inform the Commissioner of?
MS VANDENBROEK: We haven't produced a formal update to the government's
response. It's more that we're working internally and with the Minister's office on the
ways to address those recommendations.
MR LANCASTER SC: How many recommendations are the subject of further
analysis and consideration?
MS VANDENBROEK: I don't know the number to hand. I would need to look
through them to work that out. I could work that out for you. It will take me a couple
of minutes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes, thank you.
MS VANDENBROEK: There are 18 of the support in principle recommendations
where we have done further work since the government response was produced.
MR LANCASTER SC: 18 of the recommendations?
MS VANDENBROEK: Of the ones that are marked "support in principle". Of those
that are "noted" -

MR LANCASTER SC: I think 20 of the recommendations had the response support
in principle and your evidence is 18 of those 20 have been the subject of further
analysis or further consideration?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: But the final position in terms of the government's response
to those 18 recommendations has not yet been determined; is that right?
MS VANDENBROEK: Some has. I could work through them all individually, if
you would like.
MR LANCASTER SC: In terms of numbers, how many of them have been
resolved? In other words, have a government response finalised.
MS VANDENBROEK: There are a number that relate to reach and risk, and as I
think I've said in my statement, there was a position on those. It wasn't that we were
doing more work; we already had a position which was that they would be adopted
to the extent that it's about risk but not about reach. So they were supported in
principle in that they would be enacted but not exactly as the recommendation was
written. Because they are quite detailed recommendations, some, it was decided they
would be progressed but in a slightly different form to what was recommended.
MR LANCASTER SC: Do you have an estimate when a complete government
response to the Rickard Review will be prepared or finished?
MS VANDENBROEK: No, I don't, sorry.
MR LANCASTER SC: And what's the explanation for the additional time since
April that has been required when the government already had about 18 months to
respond to the review?
MS VANDENBROEK: We did a further round of consultation in relation to the
digital duty of care through May and June which helped to inform some of those
positions. We have also been progressing legal advice on some of the positions, and
the consultation particularly involved talking to the platforms about how different
things would work in practice and working in detail with the eSafety Commissioner's
team on how they would work from a regulatory perspective.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I ask you some questions about the digital duty of care,
which of course is a recommendation in the Rickard Review, but also I think
independently and before the Rickard Review was a proposal that the
Commonwealth Government had indicated it would pursue.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.

MR LANCASTER SC: There have been a series of ministerial statements of
support for the implementation of a digital duty of care?
MS VANDENBROEK: There have, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And both in the last administration and in the current
government?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: How long has the branch you supervise been considering or
developing the digital duty of care?
MS VANDENBROEK: Since it was first announced in late 2024.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, can I take you to an email, please, which has the
identifier ESC.0110.0001.1903. You see that on your screen?
MS VANDENBROEK: I can, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: It's an email from the eSafety Commissioner to a series of
departmental officers in January this year?
MS VANDENBROEK: None of those officers are in my Department. They are all
staff of the eSafety Commissioner.
MR LANCASTER SC: I see. Including the copied recipients?
MS VANDENBROEK: None of those people are in my team.
MR LANCASTER SC: I see.
MS VANDENBROEK: They are all eSafety employees.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you haven't seen the email before otherwise?
MS VANDENBROEK: No, I haven't.
MR LANCASTER SC: It refers to a meeting with the Department, you see, in the
first paragraph of the email?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And there's a reference to Mr Cole, who was acting in the
position you hold now?
MS VANDENBROEK: That's correct.

MR LANCASTER SC: And the meeting included as one of its attendees the
Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you see in the next paragraph, about halfway through,
that the meeting in January, this eSafety Commissioner email reports on the Special
Envoy being clearly frustrated when told that the digital duty of care course of action
could take up to two years for full consultation and implementation.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And is that a matter that you otherwise have an
understanding of, namely, that the Special Envoy has been pressing for a more
prompt implementation of the digital duty of care because of its particular effect in
the Jewish community?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, I am aware of that.
MR LANCASTER SC: And is it right that, as reported in this email - which of
course is not a departmental email, but the expectation in February this year, or
January this year, was that the duty of care was expected to be implemented in about
two years?
MS VANDENBROEK: The expectation was that the legislation would - the
indicative timetable is for it to be introduced by the end of this year, but there will be
a 12-month delay to the commencement of the duty of care, so that accounts for the
second year.
MR LANCASTER SC: Do you accept that is a very long timeframe in
circumstances in which the Rickard Review commenced in 2023 and reported in
2024?
MS VANDENBROEK: It is a long time, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Does the Department accept that there is an urgent need for
a better regulated online environment for the protection of the Jewish community
specifically and the community more broadly?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, we do accept that.
MR LANCASTER SC: You can understand the clear frustration of the Special
Envoy in the circumstances?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, I can.

MR LANCASTER SC: Can I take you to paragraph 74 of your first statement. Is
this still the - 74 to 77, does that still set out the presently envisaged timetable for the
implementation of the digital duty of care reforms?
MS VANDENBROEK: That is the timetable that we're working to, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Do you consider that to be realistic, optimistic, pessimistic?
MS VANDENBROEK: I think that the timetable for the drafting of the bill may be
optimistic. But I can't comment on the introduction; that's subject to parliamentary
process. That's a matter for the government that I don't have any involvement in. In
terms of the 12-month delay to take effect, that's something that we did for the social
media minimum age, in consultation with the platforms because it is - because it was
a new concept that hadn't been done before. So we accepted that it was a significant
change for the platforms to put in place.
At this point, we have been planning on a 12-month delayed effect of the digital duty
of care. It's possible that the government may decide to shorten that timeframe. That
would be a decision that we would need to seek the government's view on. It's not
something within the Department's control.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes, I was going to ask about that because the
circumstances are quite different for the digital duty of care as compared to the social
media age provisions, aren't they?
MS VANDENBROEK: It is, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Including because the social media platforms have been
well aware at least since the end of 2024 that government made a formal
commitment to proceed to implement the digital duty of care.
MS VANDENBROEK: That is correct, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And they all engaged with the Rickard Review over the
year-long consultation process that she undertook for her statutory review.
MS VANDENBROEK: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Do you consider there is a strong case for a very marked
reduction in any delayed commencement period?
MS VANDENBROEK: I think that's correct. I think when we started this process,
there wasn't the focus on the duty of care publicly and within particular groups as
what there is now. So there is probably now a case to go and re-ask the government
whether that timeframe could be realistically shortened. I don't imagine it will be
well received by the platforms, but as you say, they have been aware for a very long
time that this is coming.

MR LANCASTER SC: Indeed they have. Now, can I take you then to part of the
consultation with the social media platforms. And this is at the end of last year, the
end of 2025. I will call up a document, which is DTR.0326.0001.0676. Sorry, I gave
the wrong ID. DTR.0326.0001.0364. Yes, thank you. Have you seen this document
before, Ms Vandenbroek?
MS VANDENBROEK: I have, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: It's a summary of Digital Duty of Care Consultation?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And it takes the form of referring to various industry
roundtables and meetings on that topic and including a reference to the attendees in
each case.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And on the front page, it's a 27 November meeting with
a number of identified carriage service providers and social media platform
providers.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And a second meeting on 27 November also described as
a roundtable with some other social media and tech company attendees.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And in the second roundtable, the first bullet point refers to
a majority of stakeholders agreeing that a more formal consultation process and more
detailed proposals would be appropriate so they can make formal submissions to be
considered by government?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is it fair to say that the general approach over the platforms
over the last few years, to your observation, including at the end of 2025, has been to
ask for further rounds of consultation and consideration before government proposes
the implementation of a digital duty of care?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And so far as you are aware, have all the major platforms
taken that approach, namely, to call for further rounds of consultation and
consideration?

MS VANDENBROEK: Yes. We re-met with all of the major platforms in May and
June as part of the further consultation.
MR LANCASTER SC: In May and June this year?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And have they called for yet further consultation and -
MS VANDENBROEK: They have asked to see a draft bill when it's available.
MR LANCASTER SC: And the opportunity to make submissions and be consulted
about that?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I ask you a particular question about X Corp, and I
would call up a separate document, which is DTR.0326.0001.0672. So are you
familiar with this form of document?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: A Digital Duty of Care Consultation Survey?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Could you explain what the survey is?
MS VANDENBROEK: It was a survey that was put out publicly to capture views
about the digital duty of care. It was launched on our website. It was available for
anybody to respond to.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes. And it was a survey at the end of last year, the end of
2025?
MS VANDENBROEK: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And if we go to the final page of this document, please, you
see the top of that page, this is a survey response of X Corp completed and
submitted.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you understood before today that X Corp had
completed a survey response?

MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: This document doesn't seem to be - it's not itself signed but
it indicates that it's sent by email by an identified officer of X Corp.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And if we could go back to the first page, the format of the
survey was to ask questions and then to call for a response from whoever was
supplying it. The first question was:
"Which of the following kinds of harmful experiences or content do you think digital
platforms should take steps to prevent for young Australians under 18 years?"
And then there's a series of harmful forms of online content.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And X Corp ticked the box, "None of the above".
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Then if you go over the page to question 3, for example:
"Which of the following kinds of harmful experiences or content do you think digital
platforms should take steps to prevent for Australian adults on their platforms?"
And then there's again a series of boxes that are available to be checked for various
types of online hate speech, and violent pornography and content that
seriously - I withdraw that - content that promotes seriously harmful behaviour?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And again X Corp ticked, "None of the above".
MS VANDENBROEK: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Do you regard these responses as credible policy positions
for a mainstream social media platform to take?
MS VANDENBROEK: No, I consider those disappointing.
MR LANCASTER SC: Are you aware of other platforms taking this approach?
MS VANDENBROEK: No, I'm not.

MR LANCASTER SC: Have any other platforms gone to the length of filling out
a survey response and submitting it in the context of this survey?
MS VANDENBROEK: I don't know the answer to that.
MR LANCASTER SC: Then can we go to a separate document, please, Operator,
which is DTR.0326.0001.0676, which is a letter from X Corp to the Department
dated 5 December 2025.
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, that's a single page letter and it's signed off:
"Kind regards, X Corp."
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: It doesn't identify - or it's not signed by an identified
officer.
MS VANDENBROEK: No.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is that conventional from stakeholder corporations, or is it
peculiar to X Corp in your experience?
MS VANDENBROEK: In my experience, it's peculiar to X Corp. The major
platforms would normally have a named signatory.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, on page - it attaches a written submission, doesn't it?
MS VANDENBROEK: Yes, it does.
MR LANCASTER SC: And if we go to page 0677, when you see in the
